content: 1. The release of results from the initial phase III trials on multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB) has sparked discussions regarding the clinical relevance of the study designs and endpoints. In some cases, additional off-protocol data analyses were necessary to assess the potential added value of the experimental interventions. 2. There is a need to enhance the inclusion and separate reporting of outcomes for specific subgroups in randomized controlled trials, particularly for children, pregnant and breastfeeding women, and individuals living with HIV who are undergoing treatment. 3. Ethical considerations in tuberculosis (TB) research emphasize the principles of protecting human rights, ethics, and equity, as outlined in the WHO End TB Strategy. This principle is one of the four core tenets of the strategy. 4. Health research must adhere to international and national ethical standards, including the Nuremberg Code, the World Medical Association’s Declaration of Helsinki, and WHO’s ethical standards and procedures for research involving human participants. 5. WHO has published ethics guidance for implementing the End TB Strategy to ensure equity, human rights, and ethics are prioritized in all aspects of TB service delivery. 6. Pharmacokinetic and safety studies are essential to determine optimal drug dosing, particularly during pregnancy, and to evaluate the effects of extemporaneous manipulation of existing dosing regimens. 7. Approaches must be strengthened to ensure comprehensive recording and analysis of adverse events, including standardized data on organ class, seriousness, severity, and certainty of association. This will enable meaningful comparisons of adverse event associations with various medicines across studies, patient subgroups, and treatment regimens. 8. Research should focus on optimizing the minimum number of drugs and treatment duration, especially for patients previously treated for MDR-TB, and on addressing resistance to pyrazinamide and other medicines for which rapid molecular diagnostic methods are not yet available. 9. Further research and development are particularly needed for the following agents: Levofloxacin: Dose optimization, with new data expected from the Opti-Q study. Bedaquiline: Optimization of treatment duration in adults and children, and its use during pregnancy. Linezolid: Optimization of dose and duration in adults and children, and identification of predictors of adverse reactions. Clofazimine: Dose optimization, especially for children, and evaluation of the added value of a loading dose and drug-susceptibility testing methods. Cycloserine and Terizidone: Comparative efficacy, susceptibility testing approaches, and best practices in psychiatric care for patients on these medicines. Delamanid: Understanding its role in MDR-TB regimens, including pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics in children, people living with HIV, and pregnant women; mechanisms of drug resistance development; and optimization of treatment duration. Pyrazinamide: Development of molecular testing for resistance. Carbapenems: Further research on their role in MDR-TB regimens, including the cost-effectiveness of ertapenem as a substitute for meropenem and imipenem-cilastatin. 10. Strategies should be explored to optimize the balance of benefits and harms of treatment regimen duration through risk-stratification approaches. 11. Monitoring patient response to MDR/RR-TB treatment using culture methods is critical. Predictors and biomarkers of treatment failure and bacteriological response should be identified, particularly in subgroups such as children under 15 years, patients with extrapulmonary disease, and those on shorter MDR-TB regimens. 12. Continued evaluation of future rapid molecular testing methods is necessary, not only for diagnostic purposes but also for monitoring treatment response. 13. Engineering challenges must be addressed to develop more affordable liquid culture systems. 14. Studies should be conducted to determine the optimal timing and type of surgical interventions for patients on MDR/RR-TB treatment, as well as to improve data collection, reporting, and standardization on surgical outcomes, including long-term survival. 15. Research gaps in TB care and support, as identified in WHO guidelines, include evaluating the effectiveness of interventions to improve treatment adherence, particularly in lowand middle-income countries, and analyzing the cost-effectiveness of various incentives. 16. The effectiveness of video-supported therapy in lowand middle-income countries should be investigated, as current data are primarily from high-income settings. 17. Psychological support interventions that improve treatment adherence and health outcomes should be identified and tailored to different risk groups. 18. Models of care for TB patients should be evaluated for their risk of TB transmission in different settings, such as hospital-based versus outpatient clinics, and for their cost-effectiveness in decentralized versus centralized care. 19. Integrated treatment decision algorithms for children with presumptive pulmonary TB should undergo external validation and operational research to assess their impact and feasibility in various epidemiological and healthcare settings. 20. The use of Xpert Ultra in gastric aspirate or stool samples for diagnosing pulmonary TB in children should be evaluated for its benefits and incremental yield when combining multiple specimen types. 21. Research should focus on less invasive specimen collection methods for children, including stool testing, nasopharyngeal aspiration, and laboratory protocols that balance ease of implementation with diagnostic performance. 22. A four-month treatment regimen for children and adolescents with non-severe drug-susceptible TB should be further studied for its feasibility, societal costs, and the use of automated chest radiography software to differentiate severe from non-severe forms of TB. 23. MDR/RR-TB treatment regimens for children, including bedaquiline-containing regimens, require further evaluation for treatment outcomes, dosing optimization, cost-effectiveness, and safety. 24. Delamanid use in children should be studied for long-term safety, dosing optimization, cost-effectiveness, and mechanisms of resistance acquisition. 25. Research on TB meningitis in children and adolescents should explore the efficacy and safety of shorter intensive treatment regimens, equitable access to medicines, and the sequelae of TB meningitis, including quality of life post-treatment. 26. Models of TB care for children and adolescents should assess the cost-effectiveness, feasibility, and acceptability of decentralized, integrated, and family-centered approaches, as well as their impact on health equity and outcomes of interest. 27. Research should address the management of TB/HIV co-infection, including the timing of antiretroviral therapy initiation and the role of prophylactic corticosteroids in reducing immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome.
